sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was refused. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye goes straight to the three large numbers (3.8, 64.20, 12.4), then down to the orange bars, where Saturday is the tallest and Sunday drops off. It reads as the admin dashboard of a small bakery that sells subscriptions. It feels calm and tidy, and the warm orange suits a bakery. My assumption about the job is that the owner checks shop health at a glance. The snag comes on the second look: none of the three headline numbers has a unit.

The whole piece:
- Purpose in one sentence: yes
- Image and headline make one idea: yes. On a dashboard, the title "Shop overview" labelling the cards and chart is the right call.
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished: yes. There's no placeholder text and no misspelling.
- Same element looks the same everywhere: yes
- Mood fits the message: yes
- Headings name their sections: yes

No line came out no or unsure, so there were no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist, there is one copy point. The director may want to file it under Text or Data:
- **Headline numbers with no unit** (the KPI cards, about x 48–1232, y 145–270): "3.8" could be 3.8% or 3.8 of something else. "64.20" has no currency. "12.4" active subscribers can't be a count of people, so it is presumably 12.4k. A first-time viewer has to rebuild the meaning of all three, and "12.4 subscribers" can be read wrongly. These are the numbers the owner will act on and quote, so ambiguity here is a defect, not a style note. The fix is to put the unit on each one: 3.8%, £/$64.20, 12.4k (or the full count). It would also help to add a point of reference such as "vs August". Mark: defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The piece reads as one whole. White rounded cards on a pale grey field, one sans family, and one burnt-orange accent shared by the wordmark and the bars give it a single calm, warm mood that suits a bakery without being decorative.
- Nothing is superfluous. There are no extra rules, icons or ornament, and the section headings ("Shop overview", "Orders by delivery day") plainly name what each section holds.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Nothing in this section that matters for this piece.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One point outside this section's lines, for the director: the KPI numbers are the most prominent thing on the page, but they have no units (around x 75–620, y 195–245). "3.8" has no %, "64.20" has no currency, and "12.4" doesn't say whether it means thousands or something else. The hierarchy sends the eye straight to the three numbers that are hardest to understand. This belongs in the text section, as a defect, and it is major.

**What's working.**
- **The size steps are clear.** I can see four levels, and each one jumps clearly from the next:
  - KPI numbers: about 48 px, heavy.
  - Page title "Shop overview": about 26 px, bold.
  - Chart title "Orders by delivery day": about 17 px, semibold.
  - Labels and nav: about 15 px, regular grey. Axis labels and the source line are smaller again, about 12 px.

  No two sizes come close to colliding. The eye starts at the KPI row in the top left, then drops to the chart.
- **Weight and colour do the fine work.** The KPI labels ("Checkout conversion rate" and the others) are smaller, regular weight and grey. That puts them clearly below the numbers they label without needing another size. The chart title is the same kind of label, but it is darker and bolder, so it reads as a heading. This follows Refactoring UI's "bolder, not bigger".

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**First read.** The eye goes to the three large KPI numbers, then down to the bar chart, where the tall Saturday bar and the short Sunday bar stand out. It reads as a small e-commerce dashboard for the shop owner. It feels calm, orderly and a bit sparse.

**What it's for (assumed).** A shop owner or operator checks the shop's headline numbers and delivery-day volume at a glance.

**Walk (Arrangement and space)**
- One grid: yes. There's a 48 px page margin. The three cards sit at x 48–427, 451–829 and 853–1232, with 24 px gutters. The chart card spans the full 48–1232. The 24 px gap between the cards and the chart matches the gutter.
- Exactly aligned, no near-misses: yes. The logo, "Shop overview" and the card edges share x 48. The card labels, KPI numbers, chart title and source line share about x 74.
- Baselines across columns: yes. The three card labels and the three numbers share baselines.
- Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes. Each label sits tight on its number, and the chart title sits close to its plot. "Shop overview" is about 25 px above the cards, but it heads the whole page, so that's fine.
- One group per box: yes.
- No accidental groups: yes. The three KPI cards look alike because they are alike.
- No overlap or touching: yes.
- Margin from the page edge: yes, 48 px on the left and right.
- Empty space gathered: yes. It sits in the empty right side of the header and an 82 px band below the chart (y 718–800), and both are open screen space.
- Balance: yes. The content runs the full width and nothing pulls to one side.
- Centred or symmetric placement for a reason: yes. The three equal cards are three equal metrics, and the layout is left-aligned, not centred by habit.
- One proportion: yes. Thirds over a full-width panel.
- Eye path: yes. It goes header, then title, then the KPIs left to right, then the chart, then the source. Nothing leads off the edge.

---

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The grid is strict.** The three KPI cards (x 48–427, 451–829, 853–1232) and the full-width chart card (48–1232) share one outer edge. The 24 px gutter between cards is also the gap between the card row and the chart. The logo, page title and all card contents line up on two shared left edges (x 48 outside the cards, about x 74 inside). Because everything snaps to the same lines, the page reads as one system.
- **The grouping is clear.** Each card holds one label and its number with tight spacing inside it. The chart card keeps its title, plot and source line together. The thirds-over-full-width split matches the content: three peer metrics first, then one detailed view.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**

None. All 30 lines are yes.

Outside the checklist, one problem with the words is worth sending to the director:

- **The three big figures have no units** (cards at about x 74–620, y 195–245: "3.8", "64.20", "12.4"). These are the largest and darkest text on the page, and the eye lands on them first. A reader can't tell:
  - whether 3.8 is a percentage,
  - which currency 64.20 is in,
  - whether 12.4 means 12.4 thousand subscribers, or something else, since a count of subscribers can't be 12.4.

  Each one leaves the reader to rebuild the meaning, and they may rebuild the wrong one. These are numbers the owner will act on. 12.4 is the worst case, because "12.4 subscribers" is impossible and "12.4k" is only a guess. It also matters that nothing says what period the figures cover, or what they're compared with.

  Fix: put the unit into the figure, such as "3.8%", "£64.20" and "12.4k", or into the label. Add the period, such as "September 2026", to match the chart's source line.

  This is a defect in the copy (major). It may also belong under data or hierarchy.

**What's working.**
- **Clear type scale.** One sans family carries the whole page in about five sizes with big steps between them:
  - about 48 px bold for the figures
  - about 26 px bold for the page title
  - about 17 px bold for the chart title
  - about 15 px regular for the labels and nav
  - about 12 px grey for the axis labels and source line

  Each size has an obvious job, and weight and grey do the finer work rather than extra sizes.
- **Small text holds up.** The axis labels, day names and source line are set in a regular weight and a mid-grey that is clearly darker than pale. They stay readable without competing with the bars.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The contrast of the grey axis labels and source line, measured exactly. By eye it looks like it passes 4.5:1, but it's close enough to check in the code.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. Color is used across the page: the brand wordmark, the dark/gray text, the gray page with white cards, and the orange chart bars.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One palette doing one job.** The page uses only grays and white plus a single burnt orange. The orange appears in just two places: the "Crumbwell Bakes" wordmark (top left, about 48–208 × 18–38 px) and the seven bars (about 160–1148 × 370–636 px). Everything else is near-black text, mid-gray labels, white cards and a pale gray page. So the one warm color sits on the data, and the eye goes straight from the KPI numbers to the bars. Nothing else competes for that attention. Keep this restraint when you add status colors or a second series. Don't let a second hue creep in "for variety".
- **The wordmark orange is a little darker and redder than the bar orange.** That reads as deliberate: the bar orange is a mid-value that probably falls just short of 4.5:1 as text on white, while the darker shade holds up as type. Brand and data still read as one color family. Keep the darker shade for any orange text, and check both values with a contrast tool before you lock them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** None for this section. The only states that use color are the nav's active and hover states. "Overview" is marked with both weight and a darker color, not color alone, so it passes from the still.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies (three KPI cards and one bar chart, "Orders by delivery day").

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart name what its marks show, with axis values, units, and series labels?** No, for the headline figures. The three KPI numbers at about y 195–245 ("3.8", "64.20", "12.4") have no units and no time period. "3.8" is probably a percent, but the card doesn't say. "64.20" gives no currency. "12.4" under "Active subscribers" can't be a count of people. It most likely means 12,400 or 12.4k, but a viewer could also read it as a rate or an average. These are the numbers the owner will act on and repeat to others, so a figure that can be read two ways is a defect, not a style note. Someone who reads "12.4" as a literal count, or "3.8" as a ratio instead of a percent, misjudges the business. The bar chart itself is fine: the title and axis make clear the y-axis counts orders. Fix: put the unit and period next to each number, for example "3.8%", "£64.20" or "$64.20", "12.4k", and "Sept 2026" or "last 30 days" (Tufte, *Visual Display*, ch. 2; Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design"). **Defect. Major.**
2. **Does each headline number come with a comparison, such as a target, the previous period, or a trend?** No. None of the three cards has a change from last period, a target or a sparkline, so the owner can't tell whether 3.8% conversion is good or bad, or whether subscribers are growing. Each card has plenty of empty space to the right of the number (for example x 180–400 in the first card), so there's room. Fix: next to each number, add the change from the previous period ("+0.4 pts vs Aug") or the target, or a small sparkline (Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 2). **Convention, and it costs something here: a monitoring dashboard with bare numbers can't show the owner when to act. Major.**
3. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No. "Orders by delivery day" at (74, 327) only names the topic. The pattern in the data is that orders climb from Monday to a Saturday peak of about 1,130, roughly three times Sunday's ~380. The viewer has to work that out alone, and the Sunday drop is the operationally interesting part. Fix: a title or caption that states the point, for example "Saturday is the busiest delivery day; Sunday the quietest". This is common sense: the catalog source isn't on the approved list. **Taste. Minor:** with one series and seven bars the pattern reads quickly anyway.

**What's working.**
- The chart is honest and clean. It's a bar chart for comparing categories, the axis starts at zero, ticks go in even steps of 300, the gridlines are pale and thin, it has no frame, and one series is in one flat orange. The bars are the darkest thing in the plot, so the Saturday peak and the Sunday drop read at once without misleading the eye (Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 17.1 and 23.2).
- The days run in natural weekday order rather than sorted by value, so the weekly rhythm (rise to Saturday, then the drop) shows as a shape. A source line names the system and the month (Sept 2026), which places the chart's sample in time.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 13 yes, 3 no (axis values, units and series labels; title states the finding; headline numbers have a comparison).

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the four links in the top nav (Overview, Orders, Subscribers, Products) and probably the "Crumbwell Bakes" wordmark. There are no buttons, fields, dialogs or forms.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening? / Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** The three KPI cards (y≈145–270) don't say what period they cover or when they were last updated, and the screen has no date-range or period control. The only time reference is the chart footnote at y≈688: "orders delivered in September 2026", in the smallest grey type on the page. The owner can't tell whether 3.8, 64.20 and 12.4 are today, this month, all time or September. It is also unclear whether the cards and the chart cover the same span. To see another month they would have to leave the page or guess. The nav part of the rule does pass: "Overview" is in bold near-black against grey siblings, and the "Shop overview" heading confirms it (Nielsen, heuristic 1, visibility of system status; heuristic 7, flexibility and efficiency of use). Fix: show the period once at the page level, next to "Shop overview", as a visible control (for example "September 2026 ▾") that sets the cards and the chart together. Add "updated <time>" if the data is live. Defect. Weight: major. A dashboard whose numbers have no stated period can't be read safely.
2. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them, instead of making them hunt for it?** Each card shows a bare number with no comparison: no change from last period, no target, no trend (cards at x≈48–1232, y≈145–270). The owner opens this page to learn whether things are getting better or worse, and nothing here answers that. Is 3.8 good? Is 64.20 up? They have to remember last month's numbers or go and find them. Fix: add one comparison line under each number, such as "▲ 0.4 vs August", with a word or sign as well as colour. Whether a number has a unit or point of reference is also a Text or Data question. The director may want to merge this with those sections' findings about the missing % and £ and the ambiguous "12.4". Taste or common sense: the source entry for this line, Tognazzini's "Anticipation", is off the approved list. Weight: major.

**What's working.** The top nav follows the usual pattern: wordmark on the left, then section links in a row at the top of the page. A first-time user knows straight away that these are the four areas of the product and how they relate (Jakob's law). The current page is marked with one clear cue, bolder weight and darker colour, and the "Shop overview" heading backs it up. That is enough to tell the user where they are without extra decoration.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Target size:** the nav labels look about 20 px tall with about 26 px between them. Measure the real hit areas against WCAG 2.5.8's 24×24 px.
- **Focus:** check whether a focus indicator is visible on the nav links, at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast.
- **Hover:** check whether a hover state is shown on the grey links.
- **Clickable cards:** check whether the KPI cards or the chart bars can be clicked through to Orders or Subscribers. If they can, nothing on the screen says so.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 30 yes, 3 no (shows where the user is and what is happening; shortcuts such as filters; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 0 unsure.
